Reading the Noise Report

Every panel in a sem_noise site report, in plain language — what it measures, what a healthy one looks like, and what it means when it looks wrong.

There is no clean image. You photographed the same spot 128 times and that is all you have. Every number in the report is squeezed out of how those 128 repeats disagree with each other — which is why the report keeps insisting the average of them is not ground truth.

native — whole-pixel shifts, measured values untouched aligned — bilinear sub-pixel shifts, noise altered

Every picture below is a real panel from python -m sem_noise demo, re-plotted one per axis. The demo builds three synthetic sites with known truth: 01_white is clean Gaussian noise, 02_signal_dependent has shot noise, and 03_drift_charging drifts, charges, correlates in time and carries row noise. The pipeline recovers all of it — so "healthy" and "trouble" below are not illustrations, they are measurements of a known answer.

Figure 1 of 4 · six panels

maps.png

Pictures of the site

Six full-resolution images. The first two show what you would get by averaging; the next three show where the wobble lives; the last shows which pixels were allowed to vote.

row 1 · col 1

Unregistered mean

Did the view move while you were shooting?

Reading it
All 128 frames added up and divided by 128, with no alignment applied at all. This is exactly what a naive burst average gives you.
Trouble sign
Soft, doubled or ghosted edges. Flat areas look fine either way — motion blur only shows up where the image has structure.
Why it matters
Blur here is motion, not noise. No denoiser can put it back. Compare it against the next panel to see how much of it alignment can undo.

row 1 · col 2

Aligned repeat mean

How much did alignment buy you back?

Reading it
The same 128 frames, each shifted back onto the first one before averaging. Put this side by side with the panel to its left; the pair is the whole point.
Trouble sign
Still blurred after alignment. That means the motion was not a simple whole-frame slide — rotation, scan shear or charging distortion, none of which one shift can fix.
Why it matters
This is the closest thing you have to a clean picture, and every caption in the report goes out of its way to say it is not ground truth — it is a noisy estimate built from 128 noisy frames.

row 1 · col 3

Last quarter − first quarter

Did the specimen change while you watched it?

Reading it
Average of the last 32 frames minus the average of the first 32. Blue got darker, red got brighter, white did not change. Nothing is normalised away first.
Trouble sign
One solid colour across the whole frame, or a pattern that traces the specimen. The colour-bar range is the fastest tell: ±7 DN is noise, ±30 DN is a real change.
Why it matters
Frame 1 and frame 128 are not measuring the same thing. Any scheme that treats them as interchangeable repeats — a burst mean, a Noise2Noise pair — is quietly broken.

row 2 · col 1

Native temporal standard deviation

How much does each pixel wobble — and is it the same everywhere?

Reading it
Standard deviation across the 128 repeats, computed per pixel, using whole-pixel shifts only. Bright means that pixel is unreliable.
Trouble sign
You can see your specimen in it. Bright lines tracing edges are leftover sub-pixel motion being miscounted as noise — a slightly-moved edge looks exactly like a very noisy edge.
Why it matters
Edges are where metrology lives, so σ at the edge is the number that decides your CD precision. edge_to_flat_sigma_ratio in summary.json puts a figure on it: 1.30 for the drifting site, 1.00 for the clean one.

row 2 · col 2

Aligned temporal standard deviation

What did sub-pixel alignment do to the noise itself?

Reading it
The identical map, but frames were shifted by fractions of a pixel using bilinear interpolation. Same site, same 128 frames, different answer.
Trouble sign
A large drop is not a win. Interpolation blends neighbouring pixels, which mechanically lowers the variance and correlates adjacent pixels. Part of the 16.3 → 12.8 DN fall is real (the edge motion is gone) and part is the interpolator flattering itself.
Why it matters
For a fractional shift (fy, fx), independent white-noise variance is multiplied by ((1−fy)²+fy²)·((1−fx)²+fx²). The report prints that factor as bilinear_white_noise_variance_factor_mean and then deliberately refuses to apply it as a correction, because real SEM noise is neither white nor signal-independent.

row 2 · col 3

Native low-gradient, unclipped mask

Which pixels were actually allowed to vote?

Reading it
White pixels are flat (gradient below the median of the smoothed mean) and never hit the black or white clipping level in any accepted frame. Then one pixel of erosion is applied so edges cannot leak in.
Trouble sign
White regions that hug the edges, or a mask that is mostly black. If the mask is full of structure, every "noise" number on the next two sheets is really measuring motion.
Why it matters
Every histogram, moment, mean–variance point and Allan curve that follows is computed from these pixels only. And the two domains get two independently derived masks — which is one honest reason native and aligned numbers can differ even before any interpolation effect.

Figure 2 of 4 · four panels

registration.png

Four timelines

All four share one x-axis: acquisition index, 0 to 127. Read them as a strip chart of the run. A flat line is a good line.

row 1 · col 1

Estimated displacement from anchor

Where did the field of view actually go?

Reading it
The y and x shift of each frame relative to the first accepted one, in pixels. Red vertical lines mark frames that were thrown out for drifting too far or correlating too poorly.
Trouble sign
A steady ramp is thermal or stage drift. A sudden step is a bump. Frame-to-frame jitter is vibration. The trouble case here ramps to +2.2 px in y and −3.4 px in x — exactly the drift the generator put in.
Why it matters
This is the number that decides whether you may pair or average frames at all. It also sets up a trap: on a specimen of repeating parallel lines, cross-correlation can lock onto the wrong line and give you a confidently wrong shift. The report raises an ambiguity flag when it sees competing peaks, but it will not reject the frame for you.

row 1 · col 2

Brightness evolution

Is the picture getting brighter?

Reading it
The whole-frame mean, one dot per frame, with nothing normalised away. The title says "no normalization" because that is the point — you are meant to see the raw trend.
Trouble sign
A ramp, a step, or a slow sag. A ramp usually means specimen charging or beam-current drift; a step means something was adjusted mid-run.
Why it matters
It is the same physics as the early/late map, reduced to one number per frame so you can see when it happened rather than just where. The fitted rate lands in brightness_slope_dn_per_unit.

row 2 · col 1

Frame residual against repeat mean

Is every frame equally far from the average?

Reading it
How far each individual frame sits from the repeat mean, measured as RMS over the flat mask. Both domains are drawn, so you also see how much alignment helped each frame.
Trouble sign
A U-shape or any trend. The U is unmistakable here: the first and last frames are furthest from the mean, the middle ones closest — because brightness ramped straight through the run and the mean landed in the middle of the ramp.
Why it matters
A U means your "average" only describes the middle of your acquisition. Train a network to map any frame to that mean and you are teaching it to undo a time trend it cannot possibly see from one frame.

row 2 · col 2

Residual local translations after alignment

Does a single shift really fit the whole frame?

Reading it
After the global shift is applied, a 3×3 grid of tiles is re-registered on its own. Each dot is one tile's leftover displacement. If one translation described the whole frame perfectly, every dot would sit at zero.
Trouble sign
Dots well above zero, or a cloud that grows with acquisition index. That is a warp, not a slide — rotation, scan shear, or the specimen distorting as it charges.
Why it matters
This is a diagnosis, not a fix. No non-rigid warp is ever applied. The panel exists to tell you that your alignment model is too simple, so you can decide what to do — not to quietly paper over it.

Figure 3 of 4 · four panels

distribution.png

The shape of the noise

Now that motion has been accounted for, what is left? These four ask what the leftover wobble actually is — its shape, its tails, whether it grows with brightness, and what happens if you just subtract two frames.

row 1 · col 1

Corrected centered residual distribution

What shape is the noise?

Reading it
A histogram of (frame − repeat mean) over the sampled flat pixels. It is rescaled by √(N/(N−1)) to undo the fact that each frame helped build the mean it is being compared against. The black dashed line is a Gaussian with the same width.
Trouble sign
Fat tails, a lean to one side, or a second bump. Here the tell is different and just as useful: the two domains disagree. Bilinear interpolation blended neighbouring pixels, so the orange curve is taller and narrower than the teal one measuring the same physics.
Why it matters
A plain squared-error loss is the correct loss for Gaussian noise and the wrong one for heavy tails. If the tails are fat, a handful of outlier frames will dominate your training.

Honest caveat: both demo sites are Gaussian by construction, so neither histogram shows a fat tail. On real data this is the panel where a badly-behaved detector would finally show itself.

row 1 · col 2

Standardized Gaussian Q–Q

…and is it really Gaussian out in the tails?

Reading it
Sort your residuals; sort an equal number of ideal Gaussian values; plot one against the other. Perfectly Gaussian data lands exactly on the dashed 45° line.
Trouble sign
The ends are what matter. Bending up on the right and down on the left means heavier tails than Gaussian — more extreme values than you bargained for. Bending the other way means lighter tails. An S-curve means skew.
Why it matters
The histogram squashes the tails into a region you cannot see; the Q–Q stretches them out. Its companion number is fraction_beyond_3σ: 0.0026 measured here, against 0.0027 for a true Gaussian.

Both demo sites came out straight because every noise source the generator added was Gaussian — including the correlated and row-noise terms. The shape was never the problem on site_003; its problems are all on the next sheet.

row 2 · col 1

Signal-dependent variance

Is bright noisier than dark?

Reading it
Brightness on x, variance on y, one dot per intensity bin, with a weighted straight-line fit. The trick is that the x value comes from the even-numbered frames and the y value from the disjoint odd-numbered frames, so the two axes never share the same noise and cannot fake a correlation.
Trouble sign
A slope is not a fault — it is shot noise, and it is expected. What should worry you is a negative intercept, a fit over too narrow a signal range, or a fit the report declines to report at all. It refuses when the range is not resolved above the mean's own noise.
Why it matters
This is your empirical noise model: variance = a·signal + b, in exported DN. The README is blunt that a is not calibrated electron gain and b is not read noise, unless you can vouch for a linear raw export and a calibrated detector.

The demo checks itself here. The generator was told variance = 0.4·signal + 25. The fit came back 0.3987·signal + 25.58, R² = 0.998 — with no clean image anywhere in the calculation.

row 2 · col 2

Adjacent differences / √2

What if you just subtract consecutive frames?

Reading it
(It+1 − It)/√2 over the flat pixels. The √2 is there so that if the two frames are independent with equal variance, this curve has exactly the width of a single frame's noise — no repeat mean required.
Trouble sign
Narrower than the residual histogram from panel 1. That means consecutive frames share noise, and this estimate is biased low. The lumps on the teal curve are a second tell: whole-pixel shifts quantise the difference.
Why it matters
This is the Noise2Noise pair. If it comes out narrow, N2N is being trained on partly-shared noise and will learn to leave that shared part alone. Also note what subtraction costs you: differencing forces the result to be symmetric, so this panel cannot tell you whether the original noise was skewed.

Figure 4 of 4 · six panels

stability.png

Time and space

The most important sheet, and the least obvious. The first three ask whether frames are independent of each other in time; the last three ask whether pixels are independent of each other in space. Both questions have the same consequence: if the answer is no, averaging stops paying.

row 1 · col 1

Pixel temporal autocorrelation

Does each frame remember the one before it?

Reading it
Correlation between a pixel's value at frame t and at frame t+lag, averaged over the sampled flat pixels. Zero means the frames have no memory of each other. Excluded and missing frames are never silently closed up — pairs are taken at the true acquisition lag.
Trouble sign
Anything meaningfully above zero. The report raises a flag past 0.1 at lag 1, and the trouble site sits at 0.40.
Why it matters
Correlated frames break every pair-based estimate on the previous sheet — the adjacent-difference σ, the even/odd variance split, the assumption behind the √(N/(N−1)) correction.

The healthy curve sitting at −0.008 rather than exactly zero is expected, not a fault: subtracting a mean computed from a finite number of frames biases the autocorrelation by roughly −1/(N−1), and −1/127 = −0.0079.

row 1 · col 2 · the one that matters most

Averaging stability — pixel Allan deviation

Does averaging N frames actually help?

Reading it
On log–log axes, perfectly independent noise falls along a straight 1/√N line — that is the black dashed reference. The circles are what actually happened. The dotted purple line is a shuffled control: identical numbers, time order destroyed.
Trouble sign
The measurement leaving the dashed line, flattening out, or turning back upward. On the trouble site, 32-frame averaging measured 6.44 DN where independent noise predicts 2.23 DN — and it is climbing, so averaging more frames now makes things worse.
Why it matters
This single plot tells you where averaging stops paying, and therefore how many frames a burst-mean target is actually worth. Everything else on this sheet is a diagnosis of why this curve bends.

The shuffled control is the clever part. On the trouble site it keeps falling along 1/√N while the real curve turns up. Same pixels, same noise level, only the time order differs — which proves the failure is a time-order effect, not simply too much noise.

row 1 · col 3

Mean-intensity Allan deviation

Is the whole frame's brightness holding still?

Reading it
The identical statistic as the panel to its left, but applied to just one number per frame — the mean of the whole crop. Note the y-axis: hundredths of a DN, not tens, because averaging over every pixel in the frame kills the per-pixel noise almost entirely.
Trouble sign
A curve that rises with N. Longer blocks sit further apart in time, so if brightness is drifting, their means differ more the longer you average.
Why it matters
It separates a global illumination drift from per-pixel noise. Rising here, plus a ramp on the brightness timeline, plus a one-colour early/late map is the complete charging signature — three panels telling you the same thing three different ways.

row 2 · col 1

Detrended mean-intensity periodogram

Is there a rhythm hiding in it?

Reading it
The power spectrum of that same one-number-per-frame series, Hann-windowed and linearly detrended so the straight ramp does not swamp everything. The x-axis reads in Hz if you supplied timestamps or a frame interval, and in cycles/frame if you did not.
Trouble sign
Two different shapes mean two different things. A sharp isolated spike is a periodic disturbance at that exact rate. A smooth climb toward zero — what the trouble site shows — is slow wandering, the frequency-domain face of the correlated noise from panel 1.
Why it matters
A spike you can chase down and switch off. A low-frequency climb you cannot — it just means your frames are not independent. And one honest limit, stated plainly in the README: without pixel and line timing this cannot identify 50/60 Hz mains pickup. It only sees frame-to-frame rates.

row 2 · col 2

Native pair spatial spectrum

Does the noise have a pattern across the image?

Reading it
A 2-D power spectrum (log₁₀) of differences between adjacent frames — differencing removes the specimen and leaves the noise. The centre is coarse, slowly-varying structure; the edges are pixel-to-pixel detail. Truly white noise has no features at all.
Trouble sign
A bright line through the centre. This one is vertical, at zero horizontal frequency, spread across every vertical frequency — which is precisely what "each row carries its own offset" looks like in a spectrum. Scan-line noise.
Why it matters
A denoiser trained as if noise were white will happily leave row banding behind, because banding is not what it learned to remove. The demo added exactly one offset per row, rng.normal(0, 2, (size, 1)), and this stripe is what 2 DN of it looks like.

row 2 · col 3

Directional spatial autocorrelation

…and which direction does the pattern run?

Reading it
Correlation of the pair-difference with a shifted copy of itself, stepping along x (solid) and along y (dashed). Independent pixels give zero at every lag.
Trouble sign
A curve that settles at a constant offset instead of dropping to zero. Along x it never decays — step 1 pixel or 30, you are still inside the same row, still sharing that row's offset. Along y it is zero, because the next row got its own independent offset. That asymmetry is the diagnosis.
Why it matters
It turns the stripe you just saw into a direction and a number. The companions in summary.json are row_banding_ratio — 3.87 here against 1.00 for the clean site — and column_banding_ratio at 1.05. One is the reference value for independent pixels.

The small lag-1 spike on the orange curves is the interpolator again, not the specimen: bilinear shifting blends each pixel with its neighbour, so neighbours become slightly correlated. It shows up at lag 1 and nowhere else — the opposite of the row-noise signature, which never decays.

What the whole report is for

Before you trust a burst mean

The report never tells you the answer. It hands you the seven questions you have to answer yourself, in the order they can invalidate each other.

  1. Did it move? Displacement and local residuals. If a single shift does not fit the whole frame, nothing downstream is safe.
  2. Did it change? Early/late map, brightness, mean-intensity Allan. Three views of the same question; charging fails all three at once.
  3. Can you see the specimen in the noise map? Native σ. If yes, you are measuring motion and calling it noise.
  4. Are the frames independent? Temporal ACF. Above 0.1 at lag 1 and every pair-based estimate you have is biased low.
  5. Does averaging still pay at N? Pixel Allan deviation. Read the frame count straight off the x-axis where the curve leaves the 1/√N line.
  6. Is the noise white? Spatial spectrum and directional ACF. Row banding survives a denoiser that assumes white noise.
  7. Do the two domains agree? Every plot, both curves. Where native and aligned disagree, the interpolator is part of your answer — and the report will not decide for you which one to believe.

Panels re-plotted one per axis from output/sem-noise-demo128-final/site_00{1,2,3} — the same summary.json, maps.npz, frames.csv and local_registration.csv that sem_noise/report.py itself draws from.
healthy = 01_white · signal-dependent = 02_signal_dependent · trouble = 03_drift_charging
Reproduce: python -m sem_noise demo --output tmp/sem-noise-demo --frames 128 --size 128, then python -m sem_noise analyze --input tmp/sem-noise-demo --manifest tmp/sem-noise-demo/manifest.csv --output output/sem-noise-demo
